text.en: The Rav explains that the two sedras read right after Pesach are placed there by design: having received emunah through the matzah, a Jew is warned at once against the two things that spoil its effect.
He compares forbidden food to clogged arteries of the heart: the heart loses its chayus and feeling, which is why a person can keep Shabbos yet feel nothing in it.

The Rav likens the Satan before the geulah to a person in mortal danger whose adrenaline gives him strength he never knew he had; sensing his end, the Satan fights ferociously by flooding the market with treif.
Through the Rambam's letter the Rav shows that doubts in emunah are not purely intellectual: the questioners asked because forbidden food had made their emunah unclear.
From the story of the kernel of wheat the Rav learns that even a month of diligent effort is not enough without tefillah; a person needs both.
The first sin in the world was a sin of eating, not one of the three cardinal sins, which shows how great the power of food is.
Pharaoh's cabinet ministers over drink, bread and meat show that he understood food as the chief channel for spreading tumah, unlike a modern president whose chef is a mere employee.
Every force of evil has its counterpart in good: if tumah has its ministers over food, kedushah has them too, and these are the kashrus supervisors.
By the principle that the power of the maker is in the thing made, a supervisor's extra care puts kedushah into the food itself, as a housewife's intention puts kedushah into her Shabbos cooking.
The angels are called 'men' when they come to Avraham but 'angels' when they leave him, because his holy food fortified them in kedushah for the mission of saving Lot and the line of Mashiach.

A person's nefesh extends into his property, which is why chametz, the yetzer hara, must not even be in one's possession on Pesach; Rabbi Pinchas ben Yair's donkey would not eat untithed grain because it was part of its owner's nefesh.
Emunah is instinctive in every Jew; the mitzvah is not to acquire it but to keep it from being damaged, just as a healthy heart must be protected from clogged arteries.
The four kingdoms are like a cloud that keeps changing shape: in Avraham's day they were the four kings, in Shemini they are the four impure animals, and in Tazria they are the four kinds of nega'im.
The Masorah's sign for the 91 pesukim of Shemini, the name Ovadiah, is itself a hint that the chazir will return to kashrus, since Ovadiah was the first of Esav to become a ger and a navi.

The middle of the Torah falls at the burnt se'ir of Rosh Chodesh Nissan because the Torah is the blueprint of creation, and its center must correspond to Yerushalayim, the center of the world, and to that day, the center of time.

Shemini, which holds the middle of the Torah according to Rabbi Yehoshua, is read on the first Shabbos after Pesach, while Bereishis, the center according to Rabbi Eliezer, is read on the first Shabbos after Sukkos.
The large vav of 'gachon', the middle letter of the Torah, hints that the nachash, who now crawls on its belly, will stand upright again when Mashiach comes.
The Rav sees the calendar placement of Shemini next to Pesach as a lesson: one tells what not to eat and the other what to eat, and together they show how central food is to Yiddishkeit.
He reads the Torah's word for becoming impure through forbidden food as hinting at being stuffed up, so that holiness cannot enter.
He describes forbidden food as strengthening the yetzer hara and thereby leading to other aveiros, so it harms every area of Yiddishkeit, not only the act of eating.
He explains the Seder custom that the children should not fall asleep as the children's words to Hashem, asking Him to wake His children from the sleep of golus through the geulah.

The Rav applies the Or HaChaim's explanation of tumas ohel to childbirth: the mother's tumah is not a sign of anything wrong but the trace left by the great holiness of the child who learned Torah inside her.

The shorter tumah after a boy is not because there was less holiness but because the bris, with Eliyahu HaNavi's presence, interrupts it; the Torah places the bris right after the seven days to show this.
Just as kinship obligates a mother in mourning, it also gives her a share in the joy of her son's bris, which is why she too may eat on a postponed Tisha B'Av.
The natural law that everything returns to its source is what loshon hakodesh calls yovel, and it underlies teshuvah, the shofar and the fiftieth level reached on Pesach night.
Esav's nations write from the left because they are the impurity of Yitzchak's Din, and Yishmael's from the right because they are the impurity of Avraham's Chesed.

Aviv is read as the aleph-beis from the right, Chesed, while Tishrei's letters run the aleph-beis backwards, Din; the yud-beis in Aviv adds up to gimel and also hints at the twelve opening days of Nisan.
Shabbos holds the kedushah of acharis and Rosh Chodesh the kedushah of reishis, so a Shabbos Rosh Chodesh joins both, which Klal Yisrael has and Amalek, with a beginning but no end, lacks.

Avner was hinted in the middle letters because the first and last letters contain the whole word: a Jew who strays loses only his middle, while his beginning and end, his connection to the Avos, remain.
A mother carrying a child is like a walking beis medrash, since the child learns Torah from a malach in the womb; her tumah after birth is the emptying of that kedushah.

Eliyahu HaNavi, whose neshamah did not eat from the Eitz HaDaas, is connected to the eighth, the level of Mashiach, and wherever he comes tumah is pushed away; this is why the passuk of the yoledes mentions milah.

Like the father, mohel and sandek, the mother may eat at a bris on a postponed Tisha B'Av because her shaychus neshamah with the child shares in his simchah, and the same closeness lets Eliyahu's purity reach her.
Because of lashon hara Klal Yisrael became like a metzora sent out of Yerushalayim, and Mashiach himself sits as a metzora who cannot bring them back until the sin is repaired.
Rashi's two readings of 'shever', food and hope, are one: the food itself carried the taste and fragrance that only Yosef, the embodiment of Seder Taharos, could give it, so the grain was the hope.
The Baal HaTurim's acronym for 'zekunim' leaves out Taharos because Yosef did not need to be taught it: having been raised to a shepherd, he grasped his own seder by himself.
The six days of creation are six midos, each a channel from which both one of the shepherds' souls and one seder of Mishnah flow, so each shepherd knew his own seder without a teacher.
Avraham, as the first midah, is like the first letter of a word that contains the whole word, so he knew all the sedarim by himself while even Yaakov knew only Nashim.
The Yishmaelim, steeped in immorality and carrying foul smells, wrap themselves in an outward show of tznius, as a klipah appears pure in exactly the area where it is most spoiled.
The end is a replay of the beginning: the last generation must pass nisyonos like those of Avraham Avinu at the start of Klal Yisrael.
The Satmar Rav proves the Ba'al Shem Tov's teaching from halachah: a traveler who fixes his mind on a tree within the techum is treated as being there, though his body is far away.

Bilam and Avraham both claimed to do Hashem's will, but Bilam kept pressing Hashem to agree with him, while Avraham, who could have changed the decree with one word of tefillah, went to the Akeidah in simcha.
Reb Shraga Feivel derived from the Torah's demand for taharah in the Mikdash that Hashem prefers avodah done in purity, so a voided takanah still reveals Hashem's will.
The Rambam distinguished between what he kept himself and what he could write as halachah: a chumrah cannot be turned into a halachah.
If a mikvah can turn a ger into a Yid, it can turn a Yid into a better Yid.
Rabbeinu Tam tefillin are begun after marriage because, following the Gemara's view on learning after the chasunah, that is when a person can be more in taharah.
Since a person is where his thought is, one who davens with the Beis Hamikdash in mind is really standing there, and must therefore present himself as one who stands there.
The Gemara's traveler who fixes his Shabbos place by a distant tree may then walk into the city, showing halachically that a person's place follows his thought.
Bilaam also said he would not transgress Hashem's word, but he kept trying to change Hashem's will, while Avraham could have changed it with one word of tefillah and chose not to.
Hashem's insistence on purity in the Beis Hamikdash service reveals His desire, so even after Ezra's takanah lapsed, serving Him in taharah remains what He favors.
Rabbi Yosef Chaim Sonnenfeld reasoned that if a mikvah can turn a goy into a Yid, it can turn a Yid into a better Yid.
Rabbeinu Tam tefillin are begun after marriage for the same reason the Gemara prefers learning after marriage: one can then be in greater purity.
The Rav reads the absence of Taharos from the acronym zekunim as a sign of Yosef's greatness: Yaakov did not need to teach it to him, because Yosef's own soul was Seder Taharos.
Yaakov taught all the orders to his other sons, but seeing that Yosef mastered Taharos by himself showed him how high Yosef stood, and that is why he loved him.
Avraham could master the whole Torah alone because his middah, chesed, accompanies all the other middos, while Yitzchak's gevurah does not, so he knew by himself only Moed.
A tzaddik's soul extends into his possessions, so they are free of the decay that came into the world with death; this is why Yosef's stored grain did not rot while the Egyptians' grain did.

Yaakov's 'seeing' that there was grain in Mitzrayim was a perception of its holiness: grain with such taste and smell could only come from a tzaddik in Mitzrayim, which gave him hope that Yosef was there.
Since Yosef, who guarded the bris, is Friday, the day that prepares for Shabbos, kedushas habris is what makes a person worthy of Shabbos.

Fish need no shechitah or salting because the souls of tzaddikim who still need a small tikun are placed in fish, while the meat of an animal needs a great tikun; for this reason tzaddikim ate fish on Shabbos, a time to elevate sparks.
The word 'nefashos' in the brachah borei nefashos refers to souls that Hashem placed in foods, which enter Gan Eden when a Jew makes the brachah.
Hashem could have made man need gasoline like a car; that He gave food taste and color is His chein and chesed, and thanking Him for the taste during the meal is itself a brachah.
Even which half of an apple one keeps and which half a friend receives is hashgachah pratis: each part holds souls connected to that person's soul, tribe and family.
In one respect eating non-kosher food is worse than chillul Shabbos: chillul Shabbos does not become part of the person, while forbidden food becomes part of his bones, muscles and brain.

Adam was meant to eat from the Tree of Knowledge, which was a vine: had he waited and made wine for kiddush on Shabbos he would have taken its good, but eating on Friday, before it was permitted, like orlah, he took its bad; a Jew's kelipas nogah is rooted in that tree of good and evil.

Even a non-Jew's pity for a hungry beggar is the natural mercy Hashem placed in people and animals, and he acts on it so as not to spoil his own good mood; a Jew's mercy, even when he is unaware, is deep down for Hashem.

The Rav reads 'Bereishis' as 'bara shis', created the sixth, pointing to the sixth middah of Yosef HaTzaddik, the kedushas habris, at the very start of the Torah, just as milah was the first mitzvah given to a Jew.
Because the bris is the sixth middah, it is Friday, the preparation for Shabbos; so the bachurim who complain that Shabbos is boring lack the kedushas habris that brings a bright Shabbos.
A fine learner may still not merit the true Torah; certainty that one's Torah is true and not distorted comes only through kedushah.
Yesod comes before malchus: the one who guards the bris is called tzaddik like Yosef, and from that he merits kingship, so that people follow what he says, just as Friday leads into Shabbos HaMalkah.
An animal does not harm a person who keeps his tzelem Elokim; it attacks only when it takes him for an animal, and blemishing the bris is what loses the tzelem Elokim.

Following the Pri Tzaddik: the shekalim for the offerings Michael brings above come from the words of Jews saying Parshas Shekalim, as Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai's words turned into gold; so a Jew's speech must be holy.
Loss of desire for Torah and tefillah is like loss of appetite: the soul's natural hunger for good spiritual food is spoiled by what it has taken in.
The pain and tears of a bochur over his doubts are themselves proof that he believes; a real non-believer would be glad of them, since they would free him to do as he pleases.
Doubts in emunah are Amalek, equal to safek in gematria; just as the Torah juxtaposes 'Is Hashem among us' with 'Amalek came', the doubts will vanish when Amalek is erased.
Thoughts of heresy cannot be defeated with logic because they are not logical; they are leitzanus, the shell of Amalek the scoffer, and leitzanus does not respond to reasoning.

'Velo sasuru' means not to go exploring, like the meraglim who scouted the land: welcoming a thought and discussing it is the sin, while pushing it out is the mitzvah, hinted at by the gerish note on those words.
Just as Klal Yisrael awaits the geulah, each Jew in a period of trial awaits his private geulah, and one who conducts himself properly emerges with clearer emunah than before.

The Rav reasons that just as Kiryas Sefer held the three thousand forgotten halachos, so Chevron and the Machpela correspond to the parsha and halachos of milah, and this is why Mamre, the owner of Chevron, was the one who advised Avraham on milah.

According to the Rav, 'kings shall come from you' ends the parsha of milah and was said in Chevron, David became king in Chevron, and the Torah first calls Avraham a king when he acquires Efron's field: all because the place of milah is the place of kingship.
The Rav reads Efron as the orlah of the place of milah, whose narrow eye opposed holiness of the bris, so that buying the field from him was itself a kind of milah that revealed kingship there.
He explains that Avraham discovered the Machpela on the third day after his milah, the day of the festive meal, because the cave was the gift for the mitzvah of milah.

The Rav explains that Lavan, seeing the bracelets on beautiful Rivka, assumed Eliezer had stumbled with his eyes and so fallen into his power, and ran 'to the ayin', to the eye he thought was blemished.
He compares matching couples to a man's own business: anyone may eat or write beside him, but opening the same business intrudes; so too zivugim are Hashem's business, and no one can interfere.

The difference in the Torah's wording of the two missions follows the birds' natures: the raven, a taker, would come back to Noach until the land was fully dry, so its return could only signal dryness; the dove, a giver, would stop returning as soon as it found any food, even bitter, so its mission could only test whether the water had lessened.

The same verse, 'for the inclination of man's heart is evil', appears as the reason for the flood and for never bringing another flood, because Noach's korban reached the root where a reason for judgment becomes a reason for mercy, just as a deeper look in a sugya can turn the same sevara from chayav to patur.

A unanimous conviction acquits because the sages, who usually see Torah colored by their own soul's channel, all agreeing shows they reached the colorless root of Torah, where even a reason to convict can be turned to acquittal.

Rabbi Yehuda's ruling that chametz is removed only by burning reflects his root as a gilgul of Yehuda, the yud of Shem Havaya and the element of fire: he wants evil uprooted from its root, and that is why he gives simanim for the makos, to reach the root and draw down healing for Israel.

The mikveh's forty se'ah are Shem Havaya: four letters in plain spelling and ten in full spelling, like the reshus hayachid of Shabbos that is four wide and ten high, so whoever immerses enters the Name itself.

Breathing stops underwater, which the Rav connects to the verse about all that has the breath of life perishing in the flood: in the mikveh a person's earthly life is suspended and he comes out like one revived, a new person.

Noach's teivah, the sukkah and the mikveh are all built from halachos, and halachos are holy names; that is why the teivah's dimensions follow Shem Havaya, and why Haman's beam taken from the teivah fulfilled 'Hashem's war with Amalek'.

The spies' failure lay in whose agents they were: as agents of the people and their poor intent, they lacked Moshe's protecting power, and 'send for yourself' was Moshe's attempt to let them become his agents instead.

Following the Arizal, Yosef's 'you are spies' was a foretelling: the souls of the shevatim entered Moshe's spies to help them, and Yosef's own soul entered Menashe's spy, which is why 'the tribe of Yosef' is written there and not by Efraim.

The world is one body, and Mitzrayim is its 'ervah'; Yishmael, the waste of Avraham's chesed turned to lust, fits that land, which is why his sar took over Mitzrayim and why Yosef had to earn the title tzaddik precisely there.

Rashi's second explanation of Avraham's 'now I know' explains the first: that Avraham, who never looked, suddenly noticed Sarah's beauty was itself the sign that he had entered Mitzrayim's domain and needed a stronger guard.
The Canaanites 'buried treasures' in the land with their sins: the greater the holiness hidden in a place, the thicker the klipah over it, and only one who digs finds it.

Tamuz and Av correspond to the two eyes; the spies' sin was a sin of the eyes in those days, so Kalev and Yehoshua, who did not fail, are the roots of Moshiach ben David and Moshiach ben Yosef who rebuild what the eyes destroyed.

'Bereishis' hints at 'He created the sixth', the midda of Yosef, which is why the sixth (hakafah, aliyah, ushpizin) carries special weight, and why 'Tziyon', equal to Yosef in gematria, is where Hashem is great.

The Rav reads the halacha that tefillin must be from an animal permitted to be eaten through the lens of emunah: tefillin carry yetzias Mitzrayim, the foundation of emunah, and forbidden food damages emunah, so they cannot be written on something forbidden.

The two laws of kedushah missing from the Sefirah sedros, basar bechalav and tumas meis, are higher matters that belong to the fiftieth day, Shavuos, when the Torah came through the angels who ate meat and milk and the giving of the Torah removed death.

Eating from someone makes a person subservient to him; therefore eating the four impure animals, which carry the roots of the four kingdoms, draws a Jew back into the subjugation that yetzias Mitzrayim ended.

Following the Kli Yakar, an impure animal that shows one sign of purity is worse than one that shows none, like a hypocrite; the Rav applies this to food carrying a doubtful hechsher, which can mislead a Jew who would never eat plainly unkosher food.

A Jew is like a vessel that absorbed forbidden food: as long as its essence is not ruined it can be kashered, and the Rav says a person can likewise purge the effects through crying out to Hashem with tears.
The Rav explains that the short after-blessing asks for the mizbeach while full bentching does not, because a meal with bread, salt and all its mitzvos is itself a mizbeach.

Women's not lighting Chanukah candles is itself the fulfilment of the mitzvah's purpose: the segulah of sons who are talmidei chachamim comes from tznius, so by staying home they keep what Yehudis gave her life for.

According to the Parashas Derachim's view that the brothers had the status of bnei Noach, Dina, conceived by Rachel, remained Rachel's daughter, so Shimon was permitted to marry her as a sister from the father alone.

The holiest places are first covered by their opposite, as the shell covers the fruit and the orlah the bris; so Shechem, the place of Shem Kevod Malchuso and of Yosef, was first held by the son of Chamor the Chivi.
Shimon and Levi's killing was the real 'milah' of Shechem: since the whole people was orlah, removing them left the holy place whole, just as removing the orlah leaves a Jew whole.
Worldly desires exist only as a mashal for the love of Hashem; that is why the Midrash learns Hashem's love for Israel from the parsha of the rasha Shechem.
Even a war that is justified needs the sanction of a gadol; done on one's own, the harsh deed shapes the doer, which is how Shimon and Levi came from Shechem to the plot against Yosef.
Lavan's 'the daughters are my daughters' after Yaakov's convincing argument shows that a person's reasoning is shaped by the house he learned to think in, not by the merits of the case.

Rabbi Yehuda, who gave the plagues their simanim, is the same Tanna who holds chametz may only be destroyed by burning: as the soul of Yehuda, head of the camps and of fire, he always reaches for the root.

Following the Ba'al HaTanya, the very reason the Torah gives for the Flood becomes the reason for never bringing another, because returning to the root transforms the cause of judgment into a cause of merit.
A mikvah is an 'embassy' of the heavens: just as a country's embassy counts as its own soil, the mikvah, made of fire and water like the heavens, places the one who immerses inside the heavens.
The letters of Hashem's Name form a space four by ten, the measure of a reshus hayachid, and four times ten gives the forty se'ah of a mikvah, so immersion is immersion in the Name itself.
The Haggadah draws down the salvations of the plagues, which is why the Tanna'im compete to count more plagues: each one counted brings more salvation.
Both mikvah and 'rachitz' mean bitachon: immersing is giving oneself over to Hashem.

The Rav reads the whole layout of parshas Re'eh as a map of a Jew's path: holy eating that binds to Hashem, the fall through forbidden food that leaves one open to the meisis, and the closing aser te'aser as the teshuvah of one who breaks back through, which is greater than the tzaddik who never fell.

He explains the halacha of a bas Levi who remarried on one witness through feeling: a wife whose husband lives would sense it, so her mistake shows she lacks the sense of connection a daughter of Levi must have, the tribe that felt its bond with Hashem at the egel.
He notes that 'hapa'am yilaveh ishi elai', the verse of Levi's naming, equals in gematria 've'atem hadveikim', the verse about those who did not fall to Baal Peor.
He explains that Shemini Atzeres is not called a chag because chag comes from machog, a circle, and Shemini Atzeres stands above the cycle of the festivals.

He answers the Tzlach's question on Rosh Chodesh by explaining that melacha is a curse from Adam's eating, so a day of brachah is not harmed by the time taken for a fourth aliyah; the women's brachah from not giving to the egel spreads to their husbands.

He connects women's merit of Rosh Chodesh to their sensitivity: Rosh Chodesh, which is not yet a full Yom Tov in this time, can only be felt with a heightened feeling, the same feeling with which they sensed at the egel that one cannot be cut off from the living G-d.
Shevuah comes from sheva, seven: an oath reaches the root of a person's seven middos and binds them all to Hashem's Name, beyond any weakness in a particular middah.
Mashbia, to make swear, shares a root with mashpia, to bestow, since beis and pei interchange: making someone swear infuses him with strength from Heaven to do Hashem's will.
The Vizhnitzer Rebbe read 'lo nishba l'mirmah' as the soul's oath before birth to be a tzaddik: the one who ascends Hashem's mountain is the one who did not betray that oath.

Avraham's oath was not distrust of Eliezer: in Lavan's house, where the yetzer hara was overwhelming and Eliezer had a personal interest, only the kedushah drawn through the oath could keep him faithful.
Following the Divrei Yechezkel, the clothes Eliezer gave Rivka were a sample of the dress of Avraham's household: a message that joining that family means dressing that way.
Adam and Chava knew how to make clothes, yet Hashem made garments for them, to show that the clothing He is pleased with is not what people themselves consider sufficient.
Chanukah's 'mosif v'holech' is the model for a Jewish couple: as the Chasam Sofer ruled, a wife cannot object that her husband grew in yiras Shamayim, since a Jew must always become better.
The garments Hashem made for Adam were a measure-for-measure reward: because Adam covered Chava's shame with praise rather than blaming her, Heaven covered them with garments of honor.
Rabbi Meir's 'kosnos or' with an aleph is read as the inner insight of a person who sees through the Torah's narratives: clothing itself carries a light.
The hiddenness of the Purim miracle is not a sign of its smallness but of its greatness: its source was too high to be revealed to physical eyes.
Achashverosh's months of feasting were the gift of oneg Shabbos, taken from the Jews when they did not honor Shabbos and handed to him.
Purim comes in a masquerade because its light is too great to face directly, and drinking is like the anesthetic given before surgery so that one does not feel what is being done.
The holier a part of a person is, the more it must be covered, so the dignity of a human being is precisely in his being covered.
Vashti's fashions drew the Jewish women to the party, ending the Shabbos zemiros at home; the Rav reads the Megillah's opening as a loss of tznius that cost the Jews their Shabbos song.
